title: Intrinsic Value, Time Value and Put-Call Parity
objectives: Decompose any option premium into intrinsic value and time value
Derive put-call parity by replicating one portfolio with the other
Verify parity numerically and construct the arbitrage when it is violated
State the assumptions parity needs and how dividends shift the relation
motivation: Two desks quote the 100-strike call at 8.00 and the 100-strike put at 3.50. Is either mispriced? Put-call parity turns that question into one line of algebra: calls, puts, stock and a bond can be assembled into identical payoffs, so their prices are locked together by arbitrage. The same relation splits an option premium into intrinsic and time value and lets you synthesize any of the four instruments from the other three.

blocks.md: The **intrinsic value** of an option is what exercise would return right now: $\max(S - K, 0)$ for a call, $\max(K - S, 0)$ for a put. The remainder of the premium is **time value** - the price of not having to decide today. Options trade above intrinsic because waiting is valuable: the payoff function's kink means extra volatility can only help the holder, and time keeps that optionality alive. As expiry approaches time value decays to zero, and deep-in-the-money European options can trade barely above intrinsic.

blocks.title: Splitting two premiums with S = 105, K = 100
items: Put premium 2.90: intrinsic $= \max(100 - 105, 0) = 0$; time value $= 2.90$ - all of it.
The out-of-the-money put is pure time value; the in-the-money call is part concrete, part hope.

blocks.md: This decomposition also explains early exercise. Exercising a call on a non-dividend stock throws away its time value, so it never pays before expiry; a deep-in-the-money **American put**, by contrast, can be worth exercising early because its payoff is cash you could otherwise earn interest on.

blocks.title: Two ways to own max(S_T, K)
items: Portfolio A: buy one call and lend $K e^{-rT}$ (buy a zero-coupon bond paying $K$ at $T$). Cost today: $C + K e^{-rT}$.
Portfolio B: buy one put and one share. Cost today: $P + S$.
If $S_T \ge K$: A pays $(S_T - K) + K = S_T$; B pays $0 + S_T = S_T$. Identical.
If $S_T < K$: A pays $0 + K = K$; B pays $(K - S_T) + S_T = K$. Identical.
Same payoffs in every state, so same price today: $C + K e^{-rT} = P + S$.

blocks.caption: Put-call parity for European options, same strike and expiry, no dividends. With discrete compounding, $C - P = S - K/(1+r)^T$; dividends subtract their present value from the right side.

blocks.title: Parity in numbers: S = 100, K = 100, r = 5%, T = 1
items: If the call trades at 8.00, the put must trade at $8.00 - 4.8771 = 3.1229 \approx 3.12$.
A quoted put of 3.50 is 0.38 rich - free money is visible, which means someone will take it.

rows: Sell put, buy call, short stock, lend 95.1229

blocks.md: Every row nets to zero at expiry while \$0.38 was collected today: a **reversal** arbitrage. Run it a thousand times over and desks will do it for you within milliseconds - which is why in liquid markets parity violations are microscopic. Parity also hands you synthetics for free: long call plus short put equals a long forward struck at $K$ (its value today is $S - K e^{-rT}$), and each of $C$, $P$, $S$ can be manufactured from the other three plus borrowing or lending.

blocks.caption: Long call + short put is a synthetic long forward: the hockey sticks weld into a straight line, and the premiums' net effect just shifts the line vertically.

blocks.title: Parity is a consistency engine
blocks.md: Desks run parity checks continuously between listed calls and puts: any deviation beyond transaction costs is traded instantly (conversion/reversal). The same identity prices synthetic forwards, converts quotes between conventions, and - as you will see in the binomial lesson - provides a free sanity check on any option model you build.

blocks.title: Parity's fine print
blocks.md: Parity is exact only for European options with the same strike and expiry, no dividends, and frictionless borrowing at $r$. Dividends shift it to $C - P = S - PV(\text{divs}) - K e^{-rT}$; American features break the clean identity but leave hard bounds. Carry costs and borrow fees widen the band in which no arbitrage is profitable.

blocks.code:
import math
S, K, r, T = 100.0, 100.0, 0.05, 1.0
pv_k = K * math.exp(-r * T)
print(round(pv_k, 4))                 # 95.1229
print(round(S - pv_k, 4))             # 4.8771 = C - P under parity
C_quote, P_quote = 8.00, 3.50
arb_today = -C_quote + P_quote + S - pv_k
print(round(arb_today, 4))            # 0.3771 collected today, zero at expiry
blocks.caption: The arbitrage check: cash today, flat every scenario at expiry.

blocks.md: Put-call parity is the first genuinely load-bearing result in derivatives: one equation, no model, no volatility input, true by arbitrage alone. It says a call, a put, the stock and a bond are four instruments with only three degrees of freedom — buy any three in the right proportions and you have manufactured the fourth. Desks quote conversions and reversals off this line daily; when it holds to the tick, the market is consistent, and when it does not, either money is on the table or your inputs (rate, dividends) are wrong.

blocks.title: Worked parity check: S=100, K=95, r=5%, T=0.5
items: Parity: $C - P = S - Ke^{-rT} = 100 - 92.6544 = 7.3456$. Note what is *absent*: no volatility, no normal distribution, no Black-Scholes machinery. The spread between call and put prices is fixed by cash-and-carry arithmetic.
Suppose the put trades at 3.00. Then the call must trade at $3.00 + 7.3456 = 10.3456$.

If instead the call is quoted at 10.00 (0.35 cheap), the arbitrage is a **conversion**: buy call, sell put, short stock, lend 92.6544. At expiry the options combine into a forced sale of the stock at 95, the loan returns exactly 95, and the stock position is covered — you pocket 0.3456 today with zero future exposure.

Where does it break in practice? Early exercise (American options), dividends you did not model, borrow costs on the short leg, and the width of the bid-ask you must cross to put the package on. The parity *band* around the theoretical line is exactly those frictions priced honestly.

blocks.title: Why interviewers love this question
blocks.md: Parity separates candidates who memorised Black-Scholes from those who understand replication. If you can derive $C - P = S - Ke^{-rT}$ from two portfolios that pay the same at expiry (long call + bond vs long put + stock), you can also explain why a delta of 1 deep ITM is not a coincidence and why synthetic positions are just balance-sheet moves.

guidedExercise.prompt: With $S = 120$, $K = 115$, $r = 3\%$ (continuous), $T = 1$, the call trades at 10.00. Use put-call parity to infer the put's price. Note $e^{-0.03} = 0.970446$.
hints: First compute the discounted strike: $115 \times e^{-0.03}$.
guidedExercise.solution: $K e^{-rT} = 115 \times 0.970446 = 111.6012$. $P = 10.00 - 120 + 111.6012 = \$. The put is nearly all time value: it is 5 points out of the money, and its 1.60 premium is entirely optionality.

independentExercise.prompt: With $S = 100$, $K = 100$, $r = 5\%$ (continuous), $T = 1$, the call trades at 9.50 and the put at 6.00. Show that parity is violated, state the direction, and construct the arbitrage with its cash flow today and its payoff in both expiry scenarios. Note $e^{-0.05} = 0.951229$.
hints: If the combination is cheap, buy it and sell the expensive replica.
independentExercise.solution: Observed $C - P = 3.50$ but parity demands 4.8771 - the call is cheap / put rich by 1.3771. Arbitrage: buy the call (-9.50), sell the put (+6.00), short the stock (+100), lend $K e^{-rT}$ (-95.1229): cash today $= +1.3771 \approx +1.38$. At expiry the package is worth exactly the loan repayment in both scenarios ($S_T \ge 100$: call $S_T - 100$, stock $-S_T$, bond $+100$; $S_T < 100$: short put $-(100 - S_T)$, stock $-S_T$, bond $+100$), so the \$1.38 is riskless.

commonMistakes: Applying parity to American options as if it were exact - it gives bounds, not an identity.
Forgetting dividends: they shift $C - P$ down by their present value.
Using discrete and continuous discounting interchangeably: $K/(1+r)^T$ vs $K e^{-rT}$ differ unless $r$ is small and stated.
Confusing intrinsic value with premium: deep-ITM options still carry time value unless they are European near expiry.
realWorldApplication: Market makers arbitrage listed call/put pairs continuously, and synthetic forwards built from call-put combinations are used when futures are illiquid or when financing constraints make direct stock positions expensive.
quantFinanceApplication: Parity is the fastest unit test for any pricing implementation: price a call and a put with your model and check that $C - P$ matches $S - Ke^{-rT}$ exactly, independent of volatility.
summary: Intrinsic value = immediate exercise value; time value = premium minus intrinsic, and it is what decays.
Parity: $C + Ke^{-rT} = P + S$ for European options, same strike/expiry, no dividends.
Parity is enforced by arbitrage: sell the rich portfolio, buy the cheap replica, pocket the difference today with zero expiry exposure.
Long call + short put = synthetic long forward struck at $K$.
Dividends and American features shift or loosen the identity; friction defines the band where violations are untradeable.

quiz.prompt: European, no dividends: $S = 50$, $K = 50$, $r = 4\%$ (continuous), $T = 0.5$, call price 2.50. What is the put price? Note $e^{-0.02} = 0.9802$. (Two decimals.)
The intrinsic value of a put with strike 60 when the stock is at 55 is:
options: Cannot be determined without the premium
quiz.explanation: Intrinsic = $\max(K - S, 0) = \max(60 - 55, 0) = 5.00$ - the cash exercise would return immediately.

quiz.prompt: A call with strike 110 trades at 6.50 with the stock at 112. How much of the premium is time value?

quiz.explanation: Call minus put is a synthetic forward struck at K, worth $S - Ke^{-rT}$ today. Note it is independent of volatility.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about early exercise and time value are correct?
options: Exercising a call early on a non-dividend-paying stock throws away time value
A deep in-the-money American put can be worth exercising early
European options can be exercised at any time before expiry
Time value equals premium minus intrinsic value
quiz.explanation: Early call exercise on a non-dividend stock is never optimal (0), deep-ITM American puts capture interest on the strike (1), time value is premium minus intrinsic (3). European options expire-only by definition, so 2 is wrong.

quiz.prompt: Calls are rich relative to puts: $C - P > S - Ke^{-rT}$. Which trade captures the arbitrage?
options: Sell the call, buy the put, buy the stock, borrow $Ke^{-rT}$
Buy the call, sell the put, short the stock, lend $Ke^{-rT}$
Sell the stock and lend the proceeds
quiz.explanation: Sell the expensive side (call), buy the cheap replica components (put + stock financed by borrowing): positive cash today, zero at expiry. This is a conversion; the opposite trade is a reversal.

flashcards.back: $C - P = S - Ke^{-rT}$ (European, same strike/expiry, no dividends). With dividends: subtract $PV(\text{divs})$ from the right side.
Intrinsic = immediate exercise value $\max(S-K,0)$ or $\max(K-S,0)$; time value = premium minus intrinsic.
Long call + short put at strike K = long forward at K, worth $S - Ke^{-rT}$ today.
Never for calls on non-dividend stocks; sometimes for deep-ITM American puts (interest on the strike beats remaining time value).
